title: Coining 'Open Source': a 1998 Framing Decision, Not Just a License Choice
explainer: The term 'open source' is usually traced to a strategy session in February 1998, held shortly after Netscape announced it would release the source code for its browser, where the label was proposed (Christine Peterson of the Foresight Institute is widely credited) as a more business-friendly alternative to 'free software.' The choice of name was a deliberate attempt to reframe a community practice around shared source access as something companies and contributors alike could rally behind, which shaped the norms - public repos, visible issue trackers, contribution guidelines - that sustained contribution depends on today. It's a different thread from the 'Cathedral and the Bazaar' development-process story: this is about why the movement adopted the label and framing it still uses, not how the code gets written.
